passage:
On sports day the Class 5 relay reached its last lap and the whole school ground roared. Baljeet stood at the rope with fifty other children, shouting until his throat hurt. Someone behind pushed, so he pushed forward, and the rope sagged. Everyone chanted the runner's name, louder and louder. Baljeet never heard the teacher's whistle.

Then he felt a small elbow under his arm. Harish, from Class 2, had been squeezed against the pole and dropped his water bottle. His eyes were wide. Baljeet looked at his own hands still pressed on the rope.

“Sorry,” he said, and stepped back to make room.

qa.q: What did Harish drop?
qa.a: Harish dropped his water bottle.

qa.q: Why did Baljeet not hear the teacher's whistle?
qa.a: Baljeet was caught up in the shouting and pushing with the crowd, so the noise and excitement covered everything else.

qa.q: What choice did Baljeet make on seeing Harish squeezed against the pole?
qa.a: Baljeet said sorry and stepped back to make room.

qa.q: What might the sports day crowd have felt like to Harish, from Class 2?
qa.a: Harish probably felt squashed and scared, small among bigger children who were too excited to notice.

grounding: A child in a noisy crowd shouts and pushes with everyone else until the excitement fades and personal responsibility returns.

passage:
Payal here, the tailor's neighbour, telling what I saw at the under-14 match on the kasba ground. I stood behind the boundary rope when the home team hit a six. The crowd surged forward, and in the middle of it was Vidya, the tailor's daughter, maybe ten, jumping and screaming along with grown men. When the surge came, she pushed too and shouted words I'd never heard from her.

It's hard to say what she felt. She looked thrilled, but also not quite herself. A small boy near her lost his cap, and Vidya stepped on it without noticing. Later at the bus stand she asked me quietly, “Payal Didi, did I shout badly?” I only said, “You were part of a very loud crowd.”

qa.q: What happened to the small boy's cap?
qa.a: A small boy near Vidya lost his cap, and Vidya stepped on it without noticing.

qa.q: What does Vidya's question at the bus stand suggest about Vidya's feelings?
qa.a: It suggests Vidya felt uneasy afterwards and was unsure how much of the shouting and pushing was really Vidya's own.

qa.q: What could Payal say next to help Vidya think about the moment?
qa.a: Payal could ask what it felt like in the crowd and whether the boy with the cap was alright, and then suggest saying sorry.

qa.q: What might the small boy have felt when the cap was lost in the surge?
qa.a: The boy may have felt frightened and helpless, unable to reach the cap in the crush.

grounding: An observer describes a child swept along shouting and pushing in a match crowd, where excitement is contagious and personal responsibility fades.

passage:
The stadium in Amman was roaring. Nour, holding her father's hand, had never been to a real match. When the referee gave a penalty against their team, the crowd around her stood up and shouted words Nour was never allowed to say.
She shouted them too, at the top of her lungs. It felt like flying. Her friend Ada, beside her, was jumping and shoving forward with the men in front.
Nour pushed too, toward the railing, not thinking about anything.
Her father tightened his grip and pulled her back. “Nour. Look at me.” His voice was calm. She looked up, breathing fast. Suddenly she heard herself, and her cheeks went hot.
“We cheer,” he said. “We don't push.”

qa.q: Which city was the stadium in?
qa.a: It was in Amman.

qa.q: How did Nour feel as she shouted with the crowd?
qa.a: She felt excited and swept along, like she was flying, without thinking about herself.

qa.q: How did her father help, and why did it work?
qa.a: He held her firmly, spoke calmly and made her look at him, which broke the crowd's spell and kept her safe.

qa.q: How might Ada have felt pushing forward with the men?
qa.a: Ada was probably thrilled and carried along too, not noticing the risk of the crowd pushing.

grounding: Shows a child at a match shouting and pushing with the crowd, the crowd's energy making her own responsibility fade.

passage:
On sports day at the district stadium, the school's whole middle section rushed to the fence when the relay finished. Jahnavi was in the middle of it, screaming “Yellow House!” with two hundred others.
She didn't decide to push. It just happened. Everyone was leaning, and she leaned too. A small girl from Class 4, Vasudha, was squeezed against the fence in front of her, crying.
Jahnavi didn't even see her until Mr Rao blew his whistle and shouted, “Everybody, three steps back! Now!” The crowd stepped back. Mr Rao lifted Vasudha out and sat her down.
Jahnavi stood still, heart thumping. She had been pushing. She hadn't even noticed a person in front of her.

qa.q: Who blew the whistle?
qa.a: Mr Rao blew his whistle.

qa.q: How did Jahnavi feel once the crowd stepped back?
qa.a: She felt shaken and guilty, her heart thumping as she realised she had been pushing without noticing Vasudha.

qa.q: What did Mr Rao do that protected the children?
qa.a: He gave one clear order, three steps back, which stopped the push, and then lifted Vasudha out.

qa.q: How might Vasudha have felt squeezed against the fence?
qa.a: She was likely frightened and in pain, crying as bigger children pressed in behind her.

grounding: Shows a child swept along in a sports-day crowd, pushing without deciding to, as her own responsibility fades.

passage:
Day one of Ganesh festival: Tushar stood at the pandal with his sister Rajni, clapping to the dhol, shy and careful.
Day five, the immersion procession: The street was packed and loud. Tushar forgot to be careful. He shouted, danced, threw gulal at strangers, pushed into the thick of the dancing crowd. He lost Rajni's hand and didn't notice. It felt like the crowd was one big body, and he was just part of it.
The day after: Rajni showed him a scrape on her arm from being pushed near the lake. Their mother had found her crying by a lamp post. Tushar sat quietly on the steps. He remembered yesterday like it had happened to someone else.

qa.q: What did Rajni show Tushar the day after?
qa.a: She showed him a scrape on her arm from being pushed near the lake.

qa.q: How did Tushar feel sitting on the steps the day after?
qa.a: He felt guilty and strange, remembering the procession as if it had happened to someone else.

qa.q: What could Tushar do next time he's in a festival crowd?
qa.a: He could keep hold of Rajni's hand and agree a meeting point with her before joining the procession.

qa.q: How might Rajni have felt after losing Tushar's hand?
qa.a: She was probably scared and alone, pushed in the crowd until their mother found her crying.

grounding: Shows a child swept along in a festival crowd's energy, losing track of his sister as his sense of responsibility fades.

passage:
Mahima, you want to go to the big match? Let your Chinmay dadu tell you about the Rath Yatra when I was ten.
I went with my cousin Bablu. The drums were so loud I felt them in my teeth. When the chariot came, the whole crowd surged, and I surged with it, shouting, pushing the man in front, laughing. I didn't know why I was pushing. Everyone was, so it felt right.
Then a little girl near my feet fell. For one second I nearly kept going. Bablu grabbed my collar and yelled, "Stop!" We stood still like two rocks, and a woman scooped the girl up.
The crowd had felt like one big animal, and I had become part of it without deciding to.

qa.q: Who grabbed Chinmay's collar?
qa.a: His cousin Bablu grabbed his collar.

qa.q: How did young Chinmay feel while surging with the crowd?
qa.a: He felt thrilled and carried away, not thinking at all, until the girl fell and he felt a jolt of fear.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and what does it show?
qa.a: Bablu yelling "Stop!"; one person choosing to stand still can break the crowd's pull and protect someone.

qa.q: What might Bablu have felt in the moment of yelling "Stop!"?
qa.a: Bablu was likely alarmed and scared for the girl, but clear-headed enough to pull away from the crowd's excitement.

grounding: Shows a child in a festival crowd shouting and pushing with everyone else as crowd energy spreads and personal responsibility fades.
